segments.source: Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=430 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=720 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.
Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.
Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.
1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=430 with 500 mm: it is dry. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.
Station A is cool and dry; no other station has the same class.
Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.
Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.

Problem 41. Bottlenecks in the Yarrow–Elm exchange network
Trade and transport networks have capacities. A single narrow connection can limit a much larger network.
Goods move from Yarrow to Elm along two branches: Yarrow→Zephyr capacity 4, Zephyr→Elm capacity 3; Yarrow→Kite capacity 2, Kite→Elm capacity 5.
A branch cannot carry more than its smallest edge capacity. Independent branch capacities can be added, but a shared destination capacity can cap the total.
What is the maximum number of units that can reach Elm in one period? Identify the bottleneck(s).
1. Branch 1 is limited by min(4,3)=3. 2. Branch 2 is limited by min(2,5)=2. 3. Together the branches could carry 5 units. 4. No extra shared cap is given, so the maximum is 5.
A bottleneck is a local limit that constrains the total possible flow.
Flow network; branch capacity is a minimum along a path; total is the sum of independent branches subject to shared caps.
